wine.name: Grande Cuvée Nemea
wine.grapes: Agiorgitiko alone, as the Nemea appellation requires.
wine.sites: High vineyards of the Nemea zone on red clay, planted in 1991 and placed by the house at about 1,040 metres, where cool nights keep the grape fresh.
wine.making: Fermentation and extraction take place in stainless steel vats, and the malolactic fermentation follows in barriques. The wine then ages about twelve months in French barriques, the share of new barrels running by vintage, part of that time on light lees, and rests six months or more in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Sour cherry, red cherry and blueberry with plum and vanilla, and a savoury note of tobacco and warm earth; medium to full in body, with fresh acidity and fine, ripe tannin.
wine.ageing: Generous young yet built to keep, by the house's account; open it from about three years after the vintage, once the oak has settled, and keep a strong vintage longer.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Domaine Skouras's Grande Cuvée Nemea is Agiorgitiko alone from high vineyards on red clay, aged about a year in French barriques. It brings sour cherry, plum and vanilla over fresh acidity and fine tannin, with the freshness to stand beside a roast.
records.story: An oenologist trained in Dijon came home to the Argolid and in 1986 founded the house at Pyrgela, a village outside Argos, with rented vineyards, rented equipment and bottling by hand, as the house tells it. Its first wine, Megas Oenos, launched that year by the house's account, blended Agiorgitiko with Cabernet Sauvignon, a pairing the house counts among the first released in Greece; Decanter's guide to the Peloponnese dates the label to 1988. Nemea had been an appellation since 1971, red from Agiorgitiko alone, and the house soon looked to it. A small winery followed at Gymno, one of the two Argolida villages inside the Nemea zone, and in 2004 the house moved to a new winery at Malandreni, the other. The Grande Cuvée came in between: Agiorgitiko from vines planted in 1991, first bottled in 1996. Where Megas Oenos showed what the local grape could do beside a famous foreign one, the Grande Cuvée lets Agiorgitiko stand alone under the appellation, grown high for freshness and given French oak. It is the house's statement of what Nemea can be when the grape is grown high and given time in barrel, and the Skouras bottle a guest is most likely to meet under the Nemea name.

wine.name: Palaia Klimata Ktima Papaioannou Nemea
wine.sites: A chosen block of old vines, about forty years old by the house's sheet, in the family's own vineyards around Ancient Nemea, kept to low yields.
wine.making: A classical red fermentation at the family winery in Ancient Nemea, then ageing in oak barrels and a further spell in bottle before release. The house gives about a year in oak on one sheet and eighteen months on another, each followed by about a year in bottle, so the regime runs by vintage.
wine.glass: Ripe cherry with pepper, nutmeg, fragrant herbs and vanilla; full and rounded, with velvety tannin, balanced acidity and oak that shows in its youth.
wine.ageing: Ready to drink on release after its time in bottle; the house gives it about ten years, and a strong vintage settles its oak with time.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, the house suggesting 18; decant a young bottle for an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Ktima Papaioannou's Palaia Klimata, Old Vines on the English label, is Agiorgitiko alone from a block of old vines the family farms at Ancient Nemea. Aged in oak and then in bottle, it shows red berries, pepper and nutmeg on velvety tannin.
records.story: The Papaioannou family's merchants and a Greek gastronomy guide date its work with Agiorgitiko at Ancient Nemea to 1876, a claim the house's own pages read here do not themselves make. The family's vineyards lie around the village of Ancient Nemea, and when Nemea became an appellation in 1971, red from Agiorgitiko alone, they stood inside it. The man who built the modern estate is remembered by Wines of Greece as one of the first Greek producers to argue that a wine should keep the marks of its grape, its site and the grower's methods, and the same guide and a British importer count the estate among the first in the district to farm organically; two merchants describe its vineyards as certified organic. His son, trained as a chemist and oenologist, took on the vineyards and the cellar. The range grew into a ladder of Nemeas, each from a named part of the holding: Microclima from a single plot, Terroir from old vines at Achladia, and Palaia Klimata from another chosen block of old vines, given oak and then about a year in bottle. It shows what an old Nemea family makes of its own old Agiorgitiko, and it carries its name in three languages, so a guest may meet it as Old Vines or as Vieilles Vignes.

wine.name: Ktima Driopi Reserve
wine.sites: The Dourmiza vineyard at Koutsi, on clay loam over limestone at about 380 metres, with vines about fifty years old by the house's account, trained on a bilateral cordon.
wine.making: Made at the estate's own small winery at Koutsi, the wine is aged for twelve months in French oak barrels, about seven tenths of them new and the rest in their second use, and then rests about six months in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Black cherry, sour cherry and dried plum with violet, tobacco and cocoa; full and silky, with firm, ripe tannin and a warm finish.
wine.ageing: Built for the cellar, it opens some years after the vintage, once the new oak has settled into the fruit, and a strong vintage keeps longer.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Driopi is the Nemea estate of the Tselepos family of Mantinia, and its Reserve is Agiorgitiko alone from fifty year old vines at Koutsi, aged a year in mostly new French oak. Expect black cherry, plum and violet on silky, firm tannin.
records.story: The Tselepos family made its name with Moschofilero on the cold Mantinia plateau, where it founded its estate near Rizes in 1989. In 2003, by the family's own timeline, it reached east across the Peloponnese to Nemea, an appellation since 1971 and red from Agiorgitiko alone. There it bought an old vineyard at Koutsi, the hill village that the Wines of Greece account of Nemea singles out among the zone's slopes, and named it Ktima Driopi. The vines were about fifty years old by the house's account, at about 380 metres. Part of the land was replanted with selected, virus free clones of Agiorgitiko, the old vines were kept to low yields, and a small winery was built on the estate, so that Driopi is made where it grows rather than carried back to Arcadia. The estate gives two Nemeas, the younger Driopi Classic and the Reserve, which draws on the old vines of the Dourmiza vineyard and is given a year in French oak, most of it new. Driopi is a separate estate with its own name and its own wines, though the family's Mantinia house stands behind it. It shows how a house known first for a pale, scented white reads the red slopes of Koutsi.

wine.name: Monopati
wine.sites: Old vines on rocky ground in the Nemea zone, more than fifty years old by the house's merchants; the vineyard behind the wine has changed over the years, so take the plot from the year's sheet.
wine.making: Fermented at the family winery at Petri, then aged about sixteen months in French oak barrels, the time running by vintage, before bottling; its merchants describe the making as following French ways.
wine.glass: Sour cherry, plum and raspberry with violet, vanilla, cinnamon and bitter chocolate; full in body, with firm, ripe tannin, lively acidity and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Dense and marked by oak in youth, it wants some years in bottle; its merchants credit it with a long life, so keep a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant for an hour or two; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Aivalis is a small family winery at Petri, and Monopati, its first premium wine, is Agiorgitiko alone from old vines, aged about sixteen months in French oak. It is the dense, firm side of Nemea: sour cherry, plum and chocolate on ripe tannin.
records.story: Nemea became an appellation in 1971, red from Agiorgitiko alone, and Petri, a village of the zone in Corinthia, is one of the seventeen villages entitled to its name. The Aivalis family began its winery there in the late 1990s: 1997 by a Greek gastronomy guide and a Greek business directory, 1996 by a British critic's notes, so the record leaves the year open. Its founder set out, in the guide's words, to make high quality wines that express the terroir of the area, from chosen vineyards kept to low yields and given little fertiliser. The house is small and family run, the founder's son, an oenologist, working beside him, and it is better known to Greek merchants and critics than to wine lists abroad. Monopati came first among its premium wines, by its Greek merchants' account: Agiorgitiko from old vines on rocky ground, given long French oak, a dense and muscular reading of the grape. An even older vineyard on the Fliasian plain gave the house its wine Tessera until 2022, when, by the merchants' account, it gave its last fruit, which leaves Monopati as the house's wine of old vines that a guest is most likely to meet. It shows the powerful side of Nemea, from a family of growers rather than a large firm.

wine.name: Ammos Terra Leone
wine.sites: The family's own vineyards at Kokkinies and Stefani near Ancient Nemea, by the house's sheets.
wine.making: Five days of cold soak at 8 degrees Celsius, then a traditional red fermentation, about twenty four days on the skins in all. The house's newer sheet gives eighteen months in new barrels, mostly French with a fifth American, and six in bottle; an older one gives fourteen months in new French oak and amphorae.
wine.glass: Forest fruits and black cherry dipped in dark chocolate, with vanilla and dried fruit from long barrel ageing; full and dense, with thick tannin that wants time.
wine.ageing: Tight and marked by oak on release, its tannin wants several years in bottle; keep a strong vintage longer.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for two hours; a Bordeaux glass.

Palivou Estate in Greek; the family writes Palivos in its web address.

records.table: Palivou Estate is a family winery a short walk from the sanctuary at Ancient Nemea, and Ammos Terra Leone is its oak aged Nemea, Agiorgitiko alone from the family's own vines. Long in new barrels, it is dense and chocolatey, so decant it.
records.story: The Palivos family had grown vines around Ancient Nemea long before it built a winery, treading its grapes in a traditional stone tank, as the house tells it, in the district the ancients called the Fliasian plain. Nemea had been an appellation since 1971, red from Agiorgitiko alone, when in 1995 a modern winery took the place of the old treading tank, about 800 metres from the archaeological site of Ancient Nemea, and the family counts that year as its founding; an American importer and a Greek gastronomy guide give the same year. The estate's plain Nemea, from the Kokkinies vineyard, won its first medals with the 1996 vintage, by the house's list of awards. Ammos Terra Leone became the family's oak aged reading of the grape, from its own vineyards at Kokkinies and Stefani, and its label has carried its words in more than one order over the years, with Reserve and Single Vineyard Selection on some vintages. The founders' daughters, the third generation by the house's account, joined them in the winery. The range reaches beyond the appellation to blends of Agiorgitiko with Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah under the Peloponnese regional name, which leaves Terra Leone as the bottle that says Nemea in full, from a cellar a short walk from the sanctuary.
